questions.prompt: What is the unsigned decimal value of the binary pattern 11010110?
questions.explanation: 128 + 64 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 214. The zero bits (32 and 8 and 1) contribute nothing.
traps: Skipping a set bit, often the 16 or the 2, produces one of the other options.

questions.prompt: What is the decimal value of the hexadecimal number 0x3C?
questions.explanation: 3 × 16 + 12 = 60. The hex digit C is twelve.

questions.prompt: The range of an 8-bit two’s-complement integer is
questions.explanation: Eight bits give 256 patterns. Two’s complement spends them on −128 through 127, so there is one zero and one extra negative value.
traps: −127 to 127 describes sign-magnitude, which also has a negative zero.

traps: Stopping after the invert, and forgetting the +1, yields 11111010.

questions.prompt: Which statements about two’s complement are true?
options: There is a single representation of zero
The same adder circuit works for the signed and unsigned reading of the bits
The positive and negative ranges are exactly the same size
questions.explanation: One zero and a shared adder are the reasons this encoding won. The range is not symmetric: −128 has no positive twin in 8 bits.
traps: “Two zeros” belongs to sign-magnitude, not two’s complement.

questions.prompt: A little-endian machine stores the 16-bit value 0x1234 at address 100. Which byte is at address 100?
questions.explanation: Little-endian puts the least significant byte at the lowest address. A big-endian machine would put 0x12 there.
traps: Swapping the endian names swaps the answer.

questions.prompt: IEEE-754 stores a biased exponent mainly so that
options: The sign bit can be deleted
Exponents can be stored and ordered as an unsigned field
questions.explanation: Adding a bias (127 in binary32) turns a signed exponent into an unsigned field. Finite positive numbers then sort in the same order as their encodings.
traps: The bias is not the fraction, and it does not remove the sign bit.

questions.prompt: Add the 8-bit two’s-complement values 01111111 and 00000001. What happens?
options: Signed overflow: the bit pattern 10000000 reads as −128
No overflow: the signed result is +128
The adder cannot accept these bits
questions.explanation: 127 + 1 does not fit. The bits wrap to 10000000, which is −128 in this encoding. The carry into the sign bit and the carry out of it disagree.
traps: Reading the same bits as the unsigned value 128 and calling the signed add “fine”.

questions.prompt: Why do integer ALUs usually prefer two’s complement to sign-magnitude?
questions.answer: Negation is invert-and-add-one, there is only one zero, and one adder handles both signs.
questions.explanation: Sign-magnitude has two zeros and needs extra sign logic around the adder. Two’s complement keeps the common case on a single adder.
